newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see 1996-97 U.S. soybean stocks unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see 1996-97 U.S. soybean stocks unchanged.

text.p: The U.S. Agiculture Department will likely leave unchanged its estimate for 1996-97 U.S. soybean ending stocks on Thursday's Supply and Demand Report but new crop year-end supplies may drop, analysts said.

"I think that this year's ending stocks are going to be unchanged to maybe up a little bit depending on how much they increase imports," said Mario Balletto, oilseeds analyst with Merrill Lynch. "They'll increase crush but I think that will be offset by a decrease in exports."
USDA will release its June Supply and Demand Report on Thursday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.

Analysts expected corn stocks figures to remain virtually unchanged. Some expected wheat exports to increase but most thought USDA would wait until the quarterly stocks report, slated for release June 30, to make major changes.

Soybean stocks were again expected to be the most closely-watched figure. USDA in May forecast old crop ending stocks at 125 million bushels, the tightest in 20 years. The crop year for soybeans ends August 31.

Analysts said 1996-97 soybean export figures would fall from USDA's May projection of 895 million bushels. They pointed to soaring U.S. prices and aggressive exporting by South America. Meanwhile, domestic demand for soy products has remained strong, leading many to forecast a rise in crush.
But analysts widely expected USDA would increase its projection for imports after at least two U.S. processors, Cargill Inc and Owensboro Grain, bought South American beans.
"I think they will go up five million on crush but they ought to increase the imports five (million) too," said Sid Love, analyst for Joe Kropf and Sid Love Consulting.
In contrast, the new crop soybean ending stocks estimate could fall by as much as 30 million bushels due to deteriorating South American yields and record exports from Brazil this spring.
Several analysts noted that while Brazil and Argentina both produced bumper crops, a late dry spell sliced roughly four million tonnes off of USDA's early output projections.
Brazil has already contracted to sell a large chunk of its production to take advantage of nearby premiums and will likely need to buy more than usual this fall.
USDA in May put new crop soybean ending stocks at 260 million bushels.

"I think they'll raise new crop exports to respond to the lower South American crops from both Brazil and Argentina," said Ann Frick, oilseeds analyst with Prudential Securities. "Argentina should import U.S. beans for the first time and Brazil will probably import a record amount, I'm thinking around 1.2 million tonnes."
Several analysts said corn feed usage was likely running faster than USDA has indicated but they said USDA was unlikely to make major adjustments to the corn stocks figure.
USDA last month estimated corn ending stocks at 909 million bushels, with feed usage at 1.670 billion bushels.

"I don't know that USDA wants to do very much right now," said Doug Hjort, president of Hjort Associates. "They may wait until the quarterly stocks report at the end of the month. It would appear that we're feeding a lot more than USDA is saying now but all (USDA) will do this time around is nickel or dime the numbers."
Hjort noted corn export sales were running ahead of USDA's May outlook for 1.825 billion bushels but he said shipments were trailing expectations.
Hjort and others said USDA might raise slightly its projection for U.S. wheat exports. USDA in May put wheat ending stocks at 465 million bushels with 985 million devoted to exports.
"They may raise exports for the old crop a little bit which would cut stocks but it would be a minor cut," he said.
